items.title: 1.8 Interpreting the Relation Between a One-to-One Function and Its Inverse through Graph

blocks.text: A function has an inverse only if it is bijective, that is, both one-to-one and onto. However, if the co-domain of a function is taken equal to its range, then every value in the co-domain is already attained by the function. Therefore, the function automatically becomes onto, and only the one-to-one condition is required for the existence of its inverse.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why both conditions? The inverse \(f^{-1}\) must send every output back to exactly one input. If \(f\) is not one-to-one, some output comes from two inputs and \(f^{-1}\) would not know which to choose; for example \(f(x) = x^{2}\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) gives \(f(2) = f(-2) = 4\). If \(f\) is not onto, some value of the co-domain has no input at all.
The book's point: choose the co-domain to be the range, and onto is automatic. So in practice we only check one-to-one, for example with the horizontal line test.

The graph of a function and its inverse are related through a geometric symmetry about the line \(y = x\). This line is used because any point \((x, y)\) on a function represents an input-output pair, and for its inverse, the roles of input and output are interchanged. The line \(y = x\) is exactly the set of all points where input and output values are equal, making it the natural axis of reflection for this interchange.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Our example: \(f(x) = 2x + 3\) is one-to-one with inverse \(f^{-1}(x) = \frac{x - 3}{2}\).
\(f(1) = 5\), so \((1, 5)\) is on the graph of \(f\); and \(f^{-1}(5) = 1\), so \((5, 1)\) is on the graph of \(f^{-1}\).
The points \((1, 5)\) and \((5, 1)\) are mirror images in \(y = x\): their midpoint \((3, 3)\) lies on \(y = x\), and the segment joining them has slope \(-1\), perpendicular to \(y = x\) (slope 1).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. An inverse exists when \(f\) is one-to-one and onto; with co-domain = range, one-to-one is enough.
2. \((p, q)\) on \(f\) \(\Leftrightarrow\) \((q, p)\) on \(f^{-1}\).
3. The graphs of \(f\) and \(f^{-1}\) are reflections of each other in the line \(y = x\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Reading \(f^{-1}(x)\) as \(\frac{1}{f(x)}\). The \(-1\) means inverse function, not reciprocal.
2. Reflecting in the \(x\)-axis or \(y\)-axis instead of the line \(y = x\).
3. Trying to invert a function that is not one-to-one, such as \(x^{2}\) on \(\mathbb{R}\).
